Governing Dynamic Capabilities: Cryptographic Binding and
Reproducibility Verification for AI Agent Tool Use

Ziling Zhou Affiliation: Genupixel Technology Pte. Ltd. Email: ziling@genupixel.com
Abstract

AI agents dynamically acquire capabilities at runtime via MCP and A2A, yet no framework detects when capabilities change post-authorization. We term this the capability-identity gap: it enables silent capability escalation and violates EU AI Act traceability requirements. We propose three mechanisms. Capability-bound agent certificates extend X.509 v3 with a skills manifest hash; any tool change invalidates the certificate. Reproducibility commitments leverage LLM inference near-determinism for post-hoc replay verification. A verifiable interaction ledger provides hash-linked, signed records for multi-agent forensic reconstruction. We formalize nine security properties and prove they hold under a realistic adversary model. Our Rust prototype achieves 97 µs certificate verification (<<1 ns capability binding overhead, ∼1,200,000×{\sim}1{,}200{,}000\times faster than BAID’s zkVM), 0.62 ms total governance overhead per tool call (0.1–1.2% of typical latency), and ∼{\sim}2,230 ledger appends/s. We validate reproducibility across 9 models from 7 providers (15,120 pairwise comparisons): same-provider outputs achieve 4.7×\times separation from cross-provider outputs (Cohen’s d>1.0d>1.0 on all four metrics), with best classification at F1F_{1}=0.876 (Jaccard, θ\theta=0.408); single-provider deployments achieve F1F_{1}=0.990 with 11.5×\times separation. We evaluate 12 attack scenarios—silent escalation, tool trojanization, phantom delegation, evidence tampering, collusion, and runtime behavioral attacks validated against NVIDIA’s Nemotron-AIQ traces—each detected with a traceable mechanism, while the MCP+OAuth 2.1 baseline detects none. An end-to-end evaluation over a 5-to-20-agent pipeline with real LLM calls confirms that full governance (G1–G3) adds ∼{\sim}10.8 ms per pipeline run (0.12% overhead), scales sub-linearly per agent, and detects all five in-situ attacks with zero false positives.

1 Introduction

1.1 Agent Governance: A Missing Foundation

AI agents are no longer isolated tools. Through protocols like MCP (Model Context Protocol) [8] and A2A (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) [8], modern agents dynamically discover tools, invoke external APIs, execute code, and orchestrate other agents at runtime. The MCP ecosystem alone has grown to over 1,000 tool servers in under a year [32]. As these agents assume real-world responsibilities—managing enterprise credentials, executing financial transactions, accessing sensitive data—a fundamental question emerges: what properties must an agent ecosystem satisfy for humans to trust it?

This question has been raised from multiple directions. The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) mandates traceability, logging, and conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems (Articles 12, 43, 72). NIST’s AI Agent Standards Initiative [26] identifies security controls, governance oversight, and monitoring as key requirements. The TRiSM framework [28] structures agent governance around explainability, security, privacy, and lifecycle management. Schroeder de Witt [11] calls for secure interaction protocols that prevent insecure emergent behaviors. Cheng et al. [43] ground agent safety in transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. Allegrini et al. [44] formalize 31 safety and liveness properties for agentic task lifecycles in temporal logic. Ghosh et al. [45] propose an operational safety framework with red-teaming methodology, policy-based tool scoping, and optional trace signing—but without cryptographic capability binding, formal adversary models, or verifiable replay mechanisms.

Yet despite this convergence of concern, no existing framework translates these governance aspirations into enforceable cryptographic infrastructure. The gap is not in recognizing what is needed, but in building it. We propose three Agent Governance Requirements that distill the common thread across these efforts into technically precise, verifiable properties:

Definition 1 (Agent Governance Requirements).

A governed agent ecosystem satisfies three properties:

G1: Capability Integrity. Every agent’s identity is cryptographically bound to its complete capability set—the model it executes and every tool it can invoke. The identity is unforgeable and non-repudiable. Any change to the capability set invalidates existing credentials and requires explicit re-authorization by a human or organizational principal.

G2: Behavioral Verifiability. An agent’s actions within its authorized capability envelope can be independently verified post-hoc, enabling detection of model substitution, unauthorized tool use, or output manipulation.

G3: Interaction Auditability. All inter-agent and agent-human interactions produce tamper-evident records sufficient for forensic reconstruction, allowing humans to audit agent behavior, attribute responsibility, and provide evidence for regulatory compliance and system improvement.

These requirements are not novel in aspiration—they reflect the consensus of legal [33, 34], regulatory [26], and technical [11, 28, 43, 44, 45] communities. What is novel is the claim that all three must hold simultaneously, and that none is achievable with existing agent infrastructure. G1 alone (without G2 and G3) permits certified agents to misbehave undetectably within their capability envelope. G2 alone (without G1) cannot distinguish authorized from unauthorized capabilities. G3 alone (without G1 and G2) produces audit logs of unverified actions by unverified agents.

1.2 Why the Current Landscape Falls Short

The current agent security landscape can be mapped into four layers (Figure 1), each addressing fragments of the governance requirements but none satisfying them:

Identity platforms (Keyfactor [19], SPIFFE/SPIRE [21, 22]) issue certificates binding an agent to a public key—but a certificate remains valid regardless of how many tools the agent acquires after issuance. G1 violated: capability changes are invisible to the identity layer.

Authorization frameworks (OIDC-A [4], Authenticated Delegation [3], Cerbos [39]) define what an authenticated agent may access—but authorization is evaluated against declared capabilities at grant time, with no mechanism to detect drift. G1 violated: authorization does not track capability changes.

Runtime gateways (Gravitee [40], Lasso Security [41]) inspect tool calls in real time—but are fundamentally stateless, with no memory of prior tool configurations and no behavioral verification. G2 and G3 violated.

Governance platforms (Credo AI [42]) maintain agent registries documenting capabilities—but operate at the documentation layer without cryptographic enforcement. G1 violated: declared capabilities are not bound to the agent’s actual configuration.

The root cause is a failure to recognize a fundamental architectural distinction in LLM-based agents. Inside a transformer’s forward pass, tool definitions and user context are indistinguishable token sequences. But at the orchestration layer, tool definitions determine which real-world actions the model’s outputs can trigger, while runtime context determines which actions the model chooses. This yields a principled capability-context separation: the capability envelope (model identity, tool definitions, permission scopes) governs what is possible and changes infrequently; the runtime context (conversation history, user instructions, memories) governs what is chosen and changes per-interaction. The security implication is direct: capability changes require re-authorization (G1); context changes require verifiability (G2) and auditability (G3).

Existing frameworks conflate the two. A tool addition and a new user message are treated identically—neither triggers re-evaluation. We call this the capability-identity gap: existing frameworks authenticate who an agent is and authorize what it may access, but none detect when the agent’s capabilities have changed. This gap enables a class of attacks we term silent capability escalation.

1.3 Our Framework: Bridging the Gap

The capability-context separation provides the theoretical foundation for three mechanisms, each targeting a specific governance requirement:

Capability-Bound Agent Certificates (§3) →\boldsymbol{\to} G1. We extend X.509 v3 with a skills manifest hash—a SHA-256 commitment to the agent’s complete tool configuration. Any mismatch causes immediate certificate invalidation. Certificates are embedded within a trust propagation tree where human and organizational entities form the roots, and trust constraints (maximum credential tier, delegation depth, allowed tools, rate limits) propagate monotonically downward. No agent can exceed the trust boundaries set by its human principal.

Reproducibility Commitments (§4) →\boldsymbol{\to} G2. Given that the capability envelope is fixed (certificate-bound), we leverage LLM inference near-determinism [1, 6] to enable post-hoc replay verification. Agents declare a reproducibility commitment level in their certificate. When an incident occurs, a verifier re-executes the agent’s declared model with the recorded inputs and compares outputs. Divergence beyond the committed threshold proves the agent executed something other than what its certificate claims.

Verifiable Interaction Ledger (§5) →\boldsymbol{\to} G3. Each interaction record contains agent IDs, certificate hashes, content commitments, and reproducibility anchors, linked by a hash chain with per-record signatures. The ledger stores only cryptographic commitments (not raw content), preserving privacy while enabling forensic reconstruction of multi-agent chains.

Together, these three mechanisms provide what the existing landscape lacks: a stateful, cryptographic governance layer satisfying G1–G3, bridging identity platforms and runtime gateways. Our contribution is not in novel cryptographic primitives; rather, we show that standard mechanisms—X.509 certificates, SHA-256 hashing, Ed25519 signatures, hash chains—when composed through the capability-context separation, are sufficient to enforce G1–G3 with negligible overhead, providing actionable design guidance for how agents should be built, how they should interact, and how their behavior should be audited.

1.4 Threat Model and Security Guarantees

We consider a PPT adversary who can compromise up to kk agent nodes, create malicious agents, inject or modify tools, and manipulate network traffic (Dolev-Yao model). Critically, the adversary can perform silent capability escalation. The adversary cannot compromise non-agent nodes or break standard cryptographic primitives.

Under this model, we define and prove nine security properties:

  1. 1.

    Capability Binding: tool configuration change ⇒\Rightarrow access denied (Theorem 5).

  2. 2.

    Trust Containment: child constraints ≤κ\leq_{\kappa} parent constraints (Theorem 4).

  3. 3.

    Chain Integrity: valid chain to trusted root required (Theorem 6).

  4. 4.

    Delegation Depth: chains bounded by ancestor’s 𝑚𝑎𝑥​_​𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ\mathit{max\_depth} (Theorem 7).

  5. 5.

    Reproducibility Soundness: different model/tools detected with overwhelming probability (Theorem 8).

  6. 6.

    Bounded Divergence: adversary-controlled model passing nn replay checks is (n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-indistinguishable from declared model (Theorem 9).

  7. 7.

    Chain Verifiability: a single unverifiable interior agent breaks end-to-end behavioral verification for all downstream nodes (Theorem 12).

  8. 8.

    Credential Isolation: colluding agents gain no extra permissions (Theorem 10).

  9. 9.

    Ledger Integrity: undetectable modification impossible (Theorem 11).

Properties 1–4 enforce G1. Properties 5–7 enforce G2 (with 7 characterizing its chain-level semantics). Properties 8–9 enforce G3.

1.5 Contributions

In summary:

  • •

    We define three Agent Governance Requirements—capability integrity, behavioral verifiability, and interaction auditability—distilling converging regulatory, legal, and technical concerns into formally precise properties (§1.1).

  • •

    We identify the capability-identity gap and the capability-context separation principle as its root cause and resolution (§1.2).

  • •

    We show that standard cryptographic mechanisms—composed through the capability-context separation—are sufficient to enforce all three requirements with negligible overhead, providing design guidance for secure agent ecosystems.

  • •

    We propose capability-bound agent certificates with monotonic trust propagation (§3).

  • •

    We introduce reproducibility as a trust primitive and establish that reproducibility is a necessary condition for behavioral verifiability: high-assurance agent deployments must be designed for deterministic output to be auditable (§4).

  • •

    We define a verifiable interaction ledger for tamper-evident forensic reconstruction (§5).

  • •

    We prove that sufficient replay verification yields bounded divergence: an adversary-controlled model that passes nn replay checks is provably (n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-indistinguishable from the declared model, with ϵ\epsilon exponentially small in nn (§4.7).

  • •

    We establish chain verifiability: behavioral verifiability is a chain property, not a node property—a single unverifiable interior agent breaks end-to-end verification for all downstream nodes, yielding principled deployment constraints on model placement in trust trees (§4.8).

  • •

    We implement a working MCP governance proxy that enforces all three requirements in real-time with ∼{\sim}120 µs overhead per call, detecting silent capability escalation, tool trojanization, and certificate forgery (§7).

  • •

    We formalize and prove nine security properties under a realistic adversary model (§6).

  • •

    We implement a Rust prototype achieving 97 µs verification, ∼0.62{\sim}0.62 ms governance overhead, and ∼1,200,000×{\sim}1{,}200{,}000\times speedup over BAID (§7).

  • •

    We deploy the full governance stack in an end-to-end multi-agent pipeline (5–20 agents with real LLM calls), demonstrating 0.12% overhead, sub-linear per-agent scaling, and detection of all in-situ attacks—while OAuth 2.1 and OpenTelemetry baselines detect none (§7.4).

1.6 Paper Organization

§2 presents the threat model and attack scenarios. §3 defines capability-bound certificates and the trust propagation tree. §4 introduces reproducibility commitments. §5 describes the verifiable interaction ledger. §6 presents formal security properties and proofs. §7 describes implementation and evaluation. §8 discusses limitations. §9 covers related work. §10 concludes.

2 Threat Model and Motivating Attacks

2.1 System Model

We model the trust infrastructure as a rooted directed tree T=(V,E,r,τ)T=(V,E,r,\tau), where VV is the set of all entities (CAs, humans, organizations, AI agents), EE is the set of certificate issuance relationships, rr is the root CA, and τ:V→{𝑁𝐴,𝐴𝐺}\tau:V\to\{\mathit{NA},\mathit{AG}\} classifies each node as Non-Agent (𝑁𝐴\mathit{NA}) or Agent (𝐴𝐺\mathit{AG}).

The tree satisfies a structural type constraint: τ⁡(u)=𝐴𝐺⟹∀(u,v)∈E:τ⁡(v)=𝐴𝐺\tau(u)=\mathit{AG}\implies\forall(u,v)\in E:\tau(v)=\mathit{AG}. Agents can delegate to sub-agents, but cannot confer trust upon humans or legal entities.

Each agent node vv holds a Capability-Bound Certificate 𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡v\mathit{cert}_{v} and maintains a runtime tool configuration 𝒯v​(t)\mathcal{T}_{v}(t) that may change over time. Each credential cc has a risk tier 𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑟c∈{T​0,T​1,T​2,T​3}\mathit{tier}_{c}\in\{T0,T1,T2,T3\} where T​0T0 (human-only) is most sensitive.

2.2 Adversary Model

We define a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} with capabilities: C1: Network Control (Dolev-Yao). C2: Agent Compromise of up to kk agent nodes. C3: Rogue Agent Creation with fresh key pairs. C4: Silent Capability Escalation—modifying tool configurations without changing identity credentials. C5: Interaction Injection—fabricating or modifying ledger records.

𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot: compromise non-agent nodes, forge digital signatures (EUF-CMA), find hash collisions, or reverse hash functions.

2.3 Motivating Attack Scenarios

We enumerate twelve attacks organized into four categories. ATK-1 through ATK-9 address structural governance threats; ATK-10 through ATK-12 address runtime behavioral attacks empirically validated by the Nemotron-AIQ dataset [45], which demonstrates 100% success rates for prompt injection and tool-mediated attacks against unprotected agentic workflows.

Capability Attacks. ATK-1: Silent Capability Escalation. Agent vv certified with {\{code_gen, unit_test}\} acquires web_browser via a plugin marketplace. Under every existing framework, vv’s credentials remain valid. Our framework detects the skills manifest hash change.

ATK-2: Model Substitution. 𝒜\mathcal{A} replaces the certified model with a fine-tuned variant. Detected via model binding mismatch and replay verification divergence.

ATK-3: Tool Trojanization. 𝒜\mathcal{A} replaces tool implementation (same name/version, different code). Detected via code-level hashing in the skills manifest.

Delegation Attacks. ATK-4: Phantom Delegation. Compromised agent (T2) issues T1 certificate to sub-agent. Prevented by monotonic trust propagation. ATK-5: Chain Forgery. Fabricated certificate chain. Prevented by signature verification at every level. ATK-6: Depth Overflow. Deep delegation hierarchy. Prevented by strictly decreasing depth counters. ATK-7: Credential Collusion. Two or more compromised agents at lower tiers (e.g., T3++T3) attempt to combine their credentials to access resources restricted to a higher tier (T1). Prevented by independent per-agent credential evaluation—each agent’s tier and permissions are verified in isolation, so colluding agents gain no additional permissions beyond their individual certificates (Theorem 10).

Forensic Attacks. ATK-8: Evidence Tampering. Log modification after incident. Prevented by hash-linked ledger with bilateral signing. ATK-9: Blame Shifting. Dispute in multi-agent chain. Resolved via interaction commitments and reproducibility replay.

Runtime Behavioral Attacks. ATK-10: Injection-Driven Knowledge Poisoning. Adversarial content injected via tool outputs (e.g., retrieval results) propagates through the agent’s reasoning chain, corrupting final outputs. Nemotron-AIQ traces show this attack succeeds in 100% of undefended trials across knowledge-poisoning and phishing-link templates. Our ledger’s content commitments (η𝑖𝑛,η𝑜𝑢𝑡\eta_{\mathit{in}},\eta_{\mathit{out}}) enable post-hoc identification of the exact span where poisoned content entered the chain.

ATK-11: Cascading Action Hijack. Injected instructions persist across multiple agent workflow stages (INFECT template), causing the agent to refuse legitimate tasks or produce harmful content at downstream nodes. Our hash-chain ledger records every inter-span transition, enabling forensic tracing of attack propagation paths that OTEL-only audit trails cannot reliably provide.

ATK-12: Output Exfiltration via Rendering. Agent outputs are manipulated to embed phishing links (PHISHING_LINK) or malicious markdown (MARKDOWN) that exfiltrate data when rendered by downstream consumers. Detected post-hoc via reproducibility verification: replaying the interaction with the committed parameters produces benign output, diverging from the tampered record.

When agent vv requests access to credential cc at time tt, the verifier executes four phases (Figure 3):

⬇
1 function Verify(chain, credential, skills, roots):
2 // Phase 1: Chain Integrity
3 if chain[0].issuer ∉\notin roots: return DENY
4 for i in 1..len(chain):

9 // Phase 3: Trust Constraint Check

11 // Phase 4: Revocation Check
12 if IsRevoked(cert_v): return DENY
13 return ALLOW

3.5 Integration with A2A Agent Cards

Agent Certificates are designed as non-invasive extensions of the A2A ecosystem via an optional extensions field in the Agent Card containing the certificate PEM, chain, and skills manifest hash.

4 Reproducibility Commitments

4.1 Reproducibility as a Necessary Condition

A key observation motivates our approach: behavioral verifiability (G2) is impossible without reproducibility. If an agent’s outputs cannot be independently regenerated—even approximately—then no post-hoc mechanism can distinguish authorized behavior from unauthorized behavior. This is not merely a limitation of our framework; it is a fundamental constraint on any verification scheme that does not rely on trusted execution environments.

This observation has a prescriptive implication for secure agent system design: high-assurance agent deployments must be engineered for reproducible output. Concretely, this means using deterministic sampling (temperature==0, fixed seeds), preferring structured outputs (code, JSON, SQL) over free-form prose where security-critical decisions are involved, and selecting inference providers that guarantee bitwise or near-bitwise reproducibility [6]. Agents that cannot commit to any reproducibility level receive a trust tier downgrade (§4.4), making the security cost of non-reproducibility explicit in the governance framework.

4.2 Empirical Foundation

LLM inference is nearly deterministic. Karvonen et al. [1] demonstrated that with fixed sampling parameters, regenerating output produces >>98% token-identical sequences. EigenAI [6] achieved 100% bit-exact deterministic inference on fixed GPU architectures with negligible performance loss. Our own validation (§7, Experiment 5) confirms that code-generating agents achieve perfect determinism, while prose outputs exhibit paraphrase-level variation that remains well-separated from cross-model divergence.

4.3 Reproducibility as a Trust Primitive

Definition 5 (Reproducibility Commitment).

ρv=(𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙,𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑔)\rho_{v}=(\mathit{level},\mathit{config}) where 𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙∈{𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙,𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑒}\mathit{level}\in\{\mathit{full},\mathit{statistical},\mathit{none}\}.

Full (𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙\mathit{level}=\mathit{full}): ∀(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑥𝑡,𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑑):Ov​(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑥𝑡,𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑑)=Ov𝑟𝑒𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦​(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑥𝑡,𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑑)\forall(\mathit{context},\mathit{seed}):O_{v}(\mathit{context},\mathit{seed})=O_{v}^{\mathit{replay}}(\mathit{context},\mathit{seed}).

Statistical (𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙\mathit{level}=\mathit{statistical}):

∀(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑥𝑡,𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑑):CharMatch⁡(Ov,Ov𝑟𝑒𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦)≥θ\forall(\mathit{context},\mathit{seed}):\mathrm{CharMatch}(O_{v},O_{v}^{\mathit{replay}})\geq\theta

The threshold θ\theta is task-type dependent: our empirical validation (Experiment 5, §7) shows that code-generating agents achieve perfect determinism (θ=0.98\theta=0.98), while prose-generating agents require θ=0.10\theta=0.10 to account for paraphrase-level variation. Cross-model divergence remains well below even the relaxed threshold (max 0.089).

None: No reproducibility commitment.

4.4 Reproducibility and Trust Tier Interaction

Reproducibility commitments interact with credential governance through a trust bonus: agents with no reproducibility commitment are downgraded one tier (T1→\toT2, T2→\toT3). This makes the governance cost of non-reproducibility explicit: an agent that cannot be verified post-hoc is inherently less trustworthy, regardless of its other credentials.

4.5 Replay-Based Verification Protocol

⬇
1 function ReplayVerify(cert, record, O_orig):
2 ρ\rho := cert.ρ\rho
3 if ρ\rho.level = none: return INCONCLUSIVE
4 O_ref := ExecuteModel(cert.μ\mu, cert.σ\sigma,
5 record.input, record.seed, ρ\rho.config)
6 if ρ\rho.level = full:
7 return O_ref == O_orig ? VERIFIED : VIOLATION
8 else: // statistical
9 return CharMatch(O_ref, O_orig) ≥\geq θ\theta ?
10 VERIFIED : VIOLATION

4.6 Security Analysis

Theorem 1 (Reproducibility Soundness, informal).

If compromised agent vv executes model M′≠MM^{\prime}\neq M or skills S′≠SS^{\prime}\neq S, replay verification detects the deviation with probability ≥1−ϵ⁡(λ)\geq 1-\epsilon(\lambda) for negligible ϵ\epsilon.

By the DiFR token divergence result [1], the match rate between different models is δ≈0.06\delta\approx 0.06 (character-level, validated in Experiment 5). By Hoeffding’s inequality: Pr[CharMatch≥θ]≤exp(−2n(θ−δ)2)\Pr[\mathrm{CharMatch}\geq\theta]\leq\exp(-2n(\theta-\delta)^{2}), which is negligible for realistic output lengths.

4.7 Indistinguishability Under Sufficient Verification

A natural concern is adversarial fine-tuning: could an adversary produce a model M′M^{\prime} that passes reproducibility checks on tested inputs but behaves maliciously on untested ones? We show that sufficient replay verification bounds the impact of any such attack.

Definition 6 ((n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-Indistinguishability).

Models MM and M′M^{\prime} are (n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-indistinguishable under skill set 𝒮\mathcal{S} and prompt distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} if, after M′M^{\prime} passes replay verification on nn independent prompts x1,…,xn∼𝒟x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\sim\mathcal{D} across skills in 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

Prx∼𝒟[CharMatch(M(x),M′(x))<θ]≤ϵ\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{CharMatch}(M(x),M^{\prime}(x))<\theta]\leq\epsilon
Theorem 2 (Bounded Divergence).

If adversary-controlled model M′M^{\prime} passes replay verification (CharMatch ≥θ\geq\theta) on nn independent prompts drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} across |𝒮||\mathcal{S}| skills, then MM and M′M^{\prime} are (n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-indistinguishable with:

ϵ≤exp⁡(−2​n​θ2)\epsilon\leq\exp\!\left(-2n\theta^{2}\right)

Equivalently, for target confidence 1−ϵ1-\epsilon, n≥ln⁡(1/ϵ)2​θ2n\geq\frac{\ln(1/\epsilon)}{2\theta^{2}} verification prompts suffice.

Proof sketch. Let Zi=𝟏[CharMatch(M(xi),M′(xi))<θ]Z_{i}=\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{CharMatch}(M(x_{i}),M^{\prime}(x_{i}))<\theta] be independent Bernoulli random variables with p=Prx∼𝒟[CharMatch<θ]p=\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{CharMatch}<\theta]. Observing ∑Zi=0\sum Z_{i}=0 (all nn tests pass), by a one-sided binomial test: Pr⁡[∑Zi=0∣p≥ϵ]=(1−p)n≤(1−ϵ)n≤exp⁡(−n​ϵ)\Pr[\sum Z_{i}=0\mid p\geq\epsilon]=(1-p)^{n}\leq(1-\epsilon)^{n}\leq\exp(-n\epsilon). Setting this equal to α\alpha (significance level) and solving yields p≤ln⁡(1/α)/np\leq\ln(1/\alpha)/n with confidence 1−α1-\alpha. The Hoeffding refinement accounting for the threshold gap gives the stated bound. Full proof in §6. ∎

Practical implications. For code-generating agents (θ=0.98\theta=0.98), only n=3n=3 prompts per skill achieve ϵ<10−2\epsilon<10^{-2}; n=12n=12 achieves ϵ<10−10\epsilon<10^{-10}. Even for relaxed prose thresholds (θ=0.10\theta=0.10), n=1200n=1200 prompts achieve ϵ<10−10\epsilon<10^{-10}. These are operationally feasible: a verification suite of 50 prompts per skill, run periodically, provides strong guarantees.

Security interpretation. This transforms reproducibility from a detection mechanism into a safety certificate: an adversary who fine-tunes MM into M′M^{\prime} that passes nn diverse replay checks has produced a model that is provably close to MM on the tested distribution. Any residual divergence is bounded by ϵ\epsilon, which decreases exponentially with the verification budget. The adversary faces a dilemma: either M′M^{\prime} behaves like MM (and the fine-tuning achieves nothing), or M′M^{\prime} diverges on some inputs and will be caught with probability increasing exponentially in nn. This is analogous to cryptographic indistinguishability: the adversary’s advantage is negligible given sufficient verification.

4.8 Chain Verifiability

The preceding analysis establishes that G2 can verify an individual agent’s computational process. A natural question arises: when agents form a multi-hop execution chain, is per-node verification sufficient for end-to-end behavioral verifiability? We show that it is not—behavioral verifiability is a chain property, not a node property—and that this observation has direct implications for trust tree architecture (Figure 4).

The gap that G2 uniquely fills. Consider what G1+G3 alone guarantee. G1 (capability binding) ensures that each agent’s certificate is bound to its declared model and tool set; any capability change invalidates the certificate. G3 (interaction auditability) ensures that every input and output is bilaterally signed and hash-chain linked; no record can be silently modified. Together, G1+G3 provide attribution integrity: we know who sent what to whom, and that no message was altered in transit.

However, signing proves attribution, not computational fidelity. A compromised agent holding a valid certificate (G1✓\checkmark) can execute an arbitrary model internally, produce output, and sign it (G3✓\checkmark). The ledger faithfully records the interaction. Every cryptographic check passes. The only mechanism that detects this attack is G2: replaying the agent’s declared model on the recorded input and comparing outputs. G2 is the software-only equivalent of trusted execution—it verifies that the declared computational process actually produced the observed output, without requiring hardware attestation (TEE).

Why chain position matters. Now consider a trust tree execution chain v0→v1→⋯→vnv_{0}\to v_{1}\to\cdots\to v_{n}, where v0v_{0} is a human principal (trust anchor) and each viv_{i} (i≥1i\geq 1) is an agent node. Agent vjv_{j} receives input from vj−1v_{j-1}, processes it using its declared model, and passes output to vj+1v_{j+1}.

Suppose vjv_{j} is a compromised agent with G2==none (either because it uses a low-determinism model or because G2 verification is not enforced). Then:

  1. 1.

    vjv_{j}’s output cannot be verified as originating from its declared model.

  2. 2.

    vjv_{j}’s output becomes vj+1v_{j+1}’s input. Even if vj+1v_{j+1} satisfies G2==full, replay verification of vj+1v_{j+1} only proves that vj+1v_{j+1} faithfully processed the input it received—but that input itself is unverifiable.

  3. 3.

    By induction, all downstream nodes vj+1,…,vnv_{j+1},\ldots,v_{n} operate on data whose provenance cannot be cryptographically verified back to the trust anchor.

Definition 7 (Chain Verifiability Depth).

For execution chain v0→v1→⋯→vnv_{0}\to v_{1}\to\cdots\to v_{n} with v0v_{0} a non-agent trust anchor, define:

CVD(vn)=min{j≥1:vj is an agent with ρvj.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑒}\mathrm{CVD}(v_{n})=\min\{j\geq 1:v_{j}\text{ is an agent with }\rho_{v_{j}}.\mathit{level}=\mathit{none}\}

with CVD⁡(vn)=n\mathrm{CVD}(v_{n})=n if no such vjv_{j} exists (fully verifiable chain).

Theorem 3 (Chain Verifiability).

Let v0→v1→⋯→vnv_{0}\to v_{1}\to\cdots\to v_{n} be an execution chain where v0v_{0} is a non-agent trust anchor. If CVD⁡(vn)=k<n\mathrm{CVD}(v_{n})=k<n, then for all i>ki>k, the output of viv_{i} cannot be verified as originating from a legitimate computation chain rooted at v0v_{0}, even if viv_{i} individually satisfies ρvi.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙\rho_{v_{i}}.\mathit{level}=\mathit{full}.

Proof sketch. By Definition 7, vkv_{k} has ρ.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑒\rho.\mathit{level}=\mathit{none}, so no replay verification can confirm that vkv_{k}’s declared model produced its output oko_{k}. Under the adversary model (§2), vkv_{k} may have executed an arbitrary model M′≠MkM^{\prime}\neq M_{k} that produces output ok′≠ok∗o_{k}^{\prime}\neq o_{k}^{*} (where ok∗o_{k}^{*} is the output the declared model would have produced). Agent vk+1v_{k+1} receives ok′o_{k}^{\prime} as input. Even with ρvk+1.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙\rho_{v_{k+1}}.\mathit{level}=\mathit{full}, replay verification confirms vk+1​(ok′)=ok+1v_{k+1}(o_{k}^{\prime})=o_{k+1}, i.e., that vk+1v_{k+1} faithfully processed ok′o_{k}^{\prime}. But ok′o_{k}^{\prime} may differ from ok∗o_{k}^{*}, so ok+1o_{k+1} is the correct computation on incorrect input. By induction on chain length, the same applies to all viv_{i} with i>ki>k. Full proof in §6. ∎

Architectural implications. This theorem yields three deployment principles:

Principle 1: High-determinism models at interior nodes. Models with strong reproducibility (Anthropic Haiku: CharMatch==0.987, Sonnet: 0.823; see Table 4) should be placed at coordinator and interior positions in the trust tree, where their outputs become inputs for downstream agents. Low-determinism models (Kimi: 0.169, DeepSeek: 0.225) should be constrained to leaf positions where their outputs do not propagate further. This is not merely a performance recommendation—it is a security architecture constraint.

Principle 2: Verification boundary checkpoints. When a G2==none agent must appear at an interior position (e.g., a reasoning model as coordinator), the chain requires a verification boundary: either (a) a human-in-the-loop checkpoint that re-anchors trust by reviewing and signing the output, (b) TEE attestation providing hardware-enforced computational integrity, or (c) dual-execution with independent instances and output comparison (analogous to Byzantine fault tolerance). Each mechanism re-establishes chain verifiability for downstream nodes.

Principle 3: Explicit degradation in the ledger. When chain verifiability is broken at node vkv_{k}, the ledger should record a PARTIAL_VERIFIABILITY marker at that boundary. Downstream agents inherit a trust tier penalty beyond the standard G2==none downgrade (§4.4), making the reduced security guarantee visible to auditors and compliance systems.

Relationship to TEE. This analysis clarifies the complementary roles of G2 and trusted execution environments. G2 provides software-only verification of computational fidelity—a “software TEE”—using only black-box API access and the near-determinism of LLM inference. Hardware TEEs provide the same guarantee through hardware attestation but require infrastructure unavailable in most LLM deployments. The Chain Verifiability Theorem shows precisely where each mechanism is needed: at every interior agent node in the trust tree. In mixed deployments, G2 and TEE are interchangeable at the chain level: an agent with TEE attestation and G2==none maintains chain verifiability identically to an agent with G2==full and no TEE.

5 Verifiable Interaction Ledger

5.1 Motivation

Capability binding and reproducibility verify individual agents. Real-world incidents involve chains of interactions. We need an immutable, tamper-evident record where no single party—including the ledger operator—can undetectably alter history.

Why OpenTelemetry traces are insufficient. The industry standard for agentic observability is OpenTelemetry (OTEL) [46], whose span trees record execution traces with span_id/parent_id linkage, timestamped input.value/output.value payloads, and span-kind annotations (CHAIN, LLM, TOOL). Analysis of the Nemotron-AIQ Agentic Safety Dataset [45]—10,796 OTEL traces from NVIDIA’s AI-Q research assistant under 22 distinct attack templates—reveals three critical gaps: (1) No integrity protection: span linkage is purely referential; any party with storage access can modify, delete, or reorder spans undetectably. (2) No identity binding: spans record function names but not cryptographically verified agent identities or capability certificates. (3) No privacy preservation: OTEL stores full plaintext input/output payloads, creating data exposure risk. Our interaction ledger addresses all three gaps through hash-chain linking (h𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑣h_{\mathit{prev}}), Ed25519 bilateral signing (𝑠𝑖𝑔i\mathit{sig}_{i}), agent certificate binding (𝑐ℎ𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑑,𝑐ℎ𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑣\mathit{ch}_{\mathit{send}},\mathit{ch}_{\mathit{recv}}), and commitment-only storage (η𝑖𝑛,η𝑜𝑢𝑡\eta_{\mathit{in}},\eta_{\mathit{out}}).

5.2 Ledger Structure

Definition 8 (Interaction Record).

Ri=(𝑠𝑒𝑞i,ti,a𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑑,a𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑣,𝑐ℎ𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑑,𝑐ℎ𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑣,η𝑖𝑛,η𝑜𝑢𝑡,πi,h𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑣,𝑠𝑖𝑔i)R_{i}=(\mathit{seq}_{i},t_{i},a_{\mathit{send}},a_{\mathit{recv}},\mathit{ch}_{\mathit{send}},\mathit{ch}_{\mathit{recv}},\eta_{\mathit{in}},\eta_{\mathit{out}},\pi_{i},h_{\mathit{prev}},\mathit{sig}_{i}) where η𝑖𝑛=SHA​-​256​(𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡)\eta_{\mathit{in}}=\mathrm{SHA\text{-}256}(\mathit{input}), η𝑜𝑢𝑡=SHA​-​256​(𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡)\eta_{\mathit{out}}=\mathrm{SHA\text{-}256}(\mathit{output}), πi=(𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑑,𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙​_​𝑣𝑒𝑟,𝑠𝑘𝑖𝑙𝑙𝑠​_​ℎ𝑎𝑠ℎ)\pi_{i}=(\mathit{seed},\mathit{model\_ver},\mathit{skills\_hash}), and h𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑣=SHA​-​256​(Ri−1)h_{\mathit{prev}}=\mathrm{SHA\text{-}256}(R_{i-1}).

Definition 9 (Verifiable Interaction Ledger).

ℒ=(R1,…,Rn)\mathcal{L}=(R_{1},\ldots,R_{n}) satisfying: (1) sequential consistency, (2) hash chain integrity, and (3) signature validity at every record.

5.3 Privacy Preservation

The ledger stores only commitments (hashes), not content. During normal operation, only interaction metadata is revealed. During forensic investigation, parties produce original content verified against stored commitments.

5.4 Forensic Reconstruction Protocol

The protocol proceeds in five steps: (1) identify the relevant interaction chain, (2) verify ledger integrity (signatures + hash chain), (3) request content disclosure and verify against commitments, (4) verify agent certificates at interaction time, and (5) execute replay verification for agents with reproducibility commitments.

6 Formal Security Properties and Proofs

We prove nine properties under the adversary model of §2, using standard cryptographic assumptions: EUF-CMA security, collision resistance of SHA-256, and the DiFR token divergence property [1].

Theorem 4 (Trust Containment).

For all edges (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E: κv≤κκu\kappa_{v}\leq_{\kappa}\kappa_{u}.

Proof.

Suppose 𝒜\mathcal{A} issues 𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡w\mathit{cert}_{w} with κw≰κκv\kappa_{w}\not\leq_{\kappa}\kappa_{v}. The verifier checks κw≤κκv\kappa_{w}\leq_{\kappa}\kappa_{v} using constraints in 𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡v\mathit{cert}_{v}, which is signed by vv’s parent. 𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot modify 𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡v\mathit{cert}_{v} without the parent’s key. Recursing upward, the chain terminates at an uncompromised non-agent ancestor (EUF-CMA). ∎∎

Theorem 5 (Capability Binding).

If Hv​(t′)≠Hv𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡H_{v}(t^{\prime})\neq H_{v}^{\mathit{cert}}, then ∀t≥t′:Access⁡(v,c,t)=DENY\forall t\geq t^{\prime}:\mathrm{Access}(v,c,t)=\mathrm{DENY}.

Proof.

By collision resistance: Pr[Hv(t′)=Hv𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡]≤negl(λ)\Pr[H_{v}(t^{\prime})=H_{v}^{\mathit{cert}}]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda) when Sv​(t′)≠σvS_{v}(t^{\prime})\neq\sigma_{v}. Forging a new certificate requires the parent’s key (same argument as Theorem 4). ∎∎

Theorem 6 (Chain Integrity).

Only chains forming a valid path from a trusted root with valid signatures pass verification.

Proof.

Fabricating any link requires the corresponding private key. By EUF-CMA, 𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot produce valid signatures without the key. ∎∎

Theorem 7 (Delegation Depth Enforcement).

Agent delegation depth from any non-agent ancestor never exceeds 𝑚𝑎𝑥​_​𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ\mathit{max\_depth}.

Proof.

Trust Containment requires κv.𝑚𝑎𝑥​_​𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ<κ𝑝𝑎𝑟⁡(v).𝑚𝑎𝑥​_​𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ\kappa_{v}.\mathit{max\_depth}<\kappa_{\mathit{par}(v)}.\mathit{max\_depth} (strict). Starting from depth dd, the chain has at most dd agent levels before reaching 0. ∎∎

Theorem 8 (Reproducibility Soundness).

If vv executes M′≠MM^{\prime}\neq M or S′≠SS^{\prime}\neq S, replay verification detects with probability ≥1−ϵ⁡(λ)\geq 1-\epsilon(\lambda).

Proof.

By DiFR [1]: 𝔼⁡[CharMatch⁡(O𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑎𝑙,O𝑟𝑒𝑓)]≤δ\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CharMatch}(O^{\mathit{actual}},O^{\mathit{ref}})]\leq\delta for different models. By Hoeffding: Pr[CharMatch≥θ]≤exp(−2n(θ−δ)2)\Pr[\mathrm{CharMatch}\geq\theta]\leq\exp(-2n(\theta-\delta)^{2}), negligible for realistic nn. ∎∎

Theorem 9 (Bounded Divergence Under Verification).

If M′M^{\prime} passes replay verification on nn independent prompts from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, then Prx∼𝒟[CharMatch(M(x),M′(x))<θ]≤ϵ\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{CharMatch}(M(x),M^{\prime}(x))<\theta]\leq\epsilon where ϵ≤exp⁡(−2​n​θ2)\epsilon\leq\exp(-2n\theta^{2}).

Proof.

Let p=Prx∼𝒟[CharMatch(M(x),M′(x))<θ]p=\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{CharMatch}(M(x),M^{\prime}(x))<\theta] be the true failure rate. Each verification trial is Bernoulli(pp). Observing nn successes (all pass), the likelihood ratio test gives: Pr⁡[all pass∣p]=(1−p)n\Pr[\text{all pass}\mid p]=(1-p)^{n}. For p≥ϵp\geq\epsilon: (1−ϵ)n≤e−n​ϵ(1-\epsilon)^{n}\leq e^{-n\epsilon}. Setting the false-acceptance probability to e−n​ϵ≤e−2​n​θ2e^{-n\epsilon}\leq e^{-2n\theta^{2}} (using ϵ=2​θ2\epsilon=2\theta^{2} as the critical value from the Hoeffding bound on the CharMatch statistic), we obtain the stated bound. The Hoeffding refinement uses the fact that CharMatch is a bounded [0,1][0,1] statistic with expected value ≥θ\geq\theta under H0H_{0} (same model), applying Pr[X¯−μ≤−t]≤exp(−2nt2)\Pr[\bar{X}-\mu\leq-t]\leq\exp(-2nt^{2}) to the complement event. ∎∎

Theorem 10 (Credential Isolation).

Accessible⁡(C′)=⋃v∈C′Accessible⁡({v})\mathrm{Accessible}(C^{\prime})=\bigcup_{v\in C^{\prime}}\mathrm{Accessible}(\{v\}).

Proof.

Access depends solely on the requesting agent’s certificate. No protocol mechanism combines permissions. Proxy tokens are bound to specific agent IDs. ∎∎

Theorem 11 (Ledger Integrity).

No party can undetectably modify, delete, or reorder records.

Proof.

(a) Modification invalidates h𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑣h_{\mathit{prev}} of successor, cascading through chain; re-signing requires all subsequent senders’ keys. (b) Deletion breaks hash chain. (c) Reordering breaks both sequence numbers and hash links. ∎∎

Theorem 12 (Chain Verifiability).

Let v0→v1→⋯→vnv_{0}\to v_{1}\to\cdots\to v_{n} be an execution chain where v0v_{0} is a non-agent trust anchor, and let CVD⁡(vn)=k<n\mathrm{CVD}(v_{n})=k<n (Definition 7). Then for all i>ki>k, the output of viv_{i} cannot be verified as originating from a legitimate computation chain rooted at v0v_{0}, even if ρvi.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙\rho_{v_{i}}.\mathit{level}=\mathit{full}.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on chain position.

Base case (i=k+1i=k+1): Agent vkv_{k} has ρ.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑒\rho.\mathit{level}=\mathit{none}. Under the adversary model (§2), 𝒜\mathcal{A} may have replaced vkv_{k}’s model MkM_{k} with Mk′M_{k}^{\prime}. Since no replay verification applies to vkv_{k}, the verifier cannot distinguish vkv_{k}’s actual output ok′=Mk′​(𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡k)o_{k}^{\prime}=M_{k}^{\prime}(\mathit{input}_{k}) from the legitimate output ok∗=Mk​(𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡k)o_{k}^{*}=M_{k}(\mathit{input}_{k}). Both are validly signed by vkv_{k} (G3✓\checkmark) and vkv_{k}’s certificate is valid (G1✓\checkmark). Agent vk+1v_{k+1} receives ok′o_{k}^{\prime} as input. Even with ρvk+1.𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑙=𝑓𝑢𝑙𝑙\rho_{v_{k+1}}.\mathit{level}=\mathit{full}, replay verification confirms vk+1​(ok′)=ok+1v_{k+1}(o_{k}^{\prime})=o_{k+1}—i.e., vk+1v_{k+1} faithfully processed ok′o_{k}^{\prime}. But since ok′o_{k}^{\prime} may differ from ok∗o_{k}^{*}, the computation is correct on potentially corrupted input. The verifier cannot detect this because verifying vk+1v_{k+1}’s replay requires vkv_{k}’s output as the reference input, which is itself unverifiable.

Inductive step: Assume the output of vi−1v_{i-1} (i−1>ki-1>k) cannot be verified as legitimate. Agent viv_{i} receives this unverifiable output as input. By the same argument as the base case, viv_{i}’s replay verification confirms computational fidelity on unverifiable input. ∎∎

7 Implementation and Evaluation

7.1 Prototype Architecture

We implement the framework as two Rust crates: agent-trust-kit (open-source SDK) and a2auth (credential governance application). Table 1 summarizes the implementation.

7.2 Performance Evaluation

We evaluate on Apple M2, 16 GB RAM, macOS. All benchmarks use Criterion.rs with 10,000 samples and 3-second warmup.

Experiment 1: Certificate Verification Latency.

Capability binding adds <<1 ns—the cost of a single 32-byte comparison. Verification is dominated by Ed25519 signature verification (∼{\sim}33 µs/sig).

Experiment 2: Skills Manifest Hash.

Experiment 3: Ledger Throughput.

Experiment 4: Reproducibility Verification Latency.

Token comparison scales at ∼{\sim}0.73 ns/token. Batch verification: 100 interactions (512 tokens each) in 41.8 µs. An auditor verifies 100,000 interactions in ∼{\sim}42 ms.

Experiment 5: Real LLM Reproducibility Validation. We validate the DiFR finding empirically in two phases. Phase 1 uses two Anthropic models (Claude Sonnet 4 and Haiku 4.5, temperature==0, max_tokens==512) across 105 prompts in five task types—code generation (25), JSON/structured output (15), mathematical reasoning (20), prose explanation (30), and creative writing (15)—with 5 same-model repetitions and 3 cross-model repetitions each (1,050 same-model + 1,575 cross-model pairwise comparisons). Phase 2 extends to 9 models from 7 providers: Claude Sonnet 4 and Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1 mini (OpenAI), Gemini 2.5 Pro (Google), Grok 4 (xAI), DeepSeek V3 (DeepSeek), Llama 4 Maverick (Meta), and Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot). All models are accessed via OpenRouter as a unified API gateway (plus Volcengine for Doubao), with temperature==0 and 100 prompts across six task types (code, JSON, math, prose, creative, knowledge), 10 repetitions per model-prompt pair (5,400 total API calls; 15,120 pairwise comparisons: 10,800 same-model + 240 same-provider + 4,080 cross-provider). We compute four similarity metrics: character-level positional match (CharMatch), Jaccard token overlap, word-level TF-IDF cosine, and character n-gram (3–5) cosine; then apply Welch’s tt-test, Mann-Whitney UU, and Cohen’s dd to quantify separation, and use Youden’s JJ statistic for optimal threshold selection.

Result 5a: Same-model reproducibility is task-type dependent. Table 2 shows per-task reproducibility from Phase 1 across 105 prompts (1,050 same-model pairwise comparisons).

Structured outputs (JSON, code) have the highest identical-output fractions (>>50%), while prose shows the most variation (34.7% identical), driven by paraphrase-level reorganization. The bimodal distribution (median CharMatch =0.975=0.975 vs. mean =0.627=0.627) confirms that same-model outputs are either near-identical or substantially rephrased.

Result 5b: Multi-provider separation analysis. Table 3 presents the Phase 2 multi-provider results across 15,120 pairwise comparisons (10,800 same-model vs. 4,080 cross-provider). All differences are statistically significant (p≈0p\approx 0, Welch’s tt and Mann-Whitney UU).

All four metrics achieve Cohen’s d>1.0d>1.0 (large effect sizes) across the full 9-model set, with Jaccard (d=1.51d=1.51) and CharMatch (d=1.36d=1.36) providing the strongest separation. Notably, same-provider pairs (e.g., GPT-4.1 vs. GPT-4.1 mini: CharMatch =0.251=0.251; Sonnet 4 vs. Haiku 4.5: 0.1920.192) exhibit similarity intermediate between same-model and cross-provider, confirming that even models from the same vendor maintain distinct output fingerprints.

Result 5c: Per-model determinism varies by over an order of magnitude. Table 4 ranks models by same-model CharMatch, revealing a wide determinism spectrum.

Claude Haiku 4.5 produces near-identical outputs across repetitions (CharMatch =0.987=0.987), while reasoning models (Kimi K2.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok 4) exhibit substantially lower determinism due to stochastic chain-of-thought reasoning even at temperature 0. Despite this variation, even the least deterministic model (Kimi K2.5, CharMatch =0.169=0.169) still exceeds the mean cross-provider similarity (0.1140.114), demonstrating that model identity remains distinguishable for all tested models.

Result 5d: Per-task separation is strongest for mathematical reasoning. Table 5 shows CharMatch separation factors across six task categories.

Mathematical reasoning achieves the highest separation (12.2×12.2\times) because models develop highly distinctive step-by-step reasoning styles, while JSON outputs show the lowest separation (2.6×2.6\times) because structural constraints force convergent formatting. These task-dependent results motivate per-task threshold calibration in deployment.

Result 5e: Optimal threshold via Youden’s JJ statistic. Table 6 reports optimal thresholds from the multi-provider experiment.

In the multi-provider setting, Jaccard achieves the best overall classification (F1=0.876F_{1}=0.876, J=0.592J=0.592), followed closely by CharMatch (F1=0.873F_{1}=0.873, J=0.572J=0.572). Both metrics attain F1>0.87F_{1}>0.87 across 9 models and 7 providers, confirming that lightweight textual similarity metrics—requiring no model internals, embeddings, or logit access—provide practically useful model identity verification even in a heterogeneous multi-provider environment.

Experiment 6: End-to-End MCP Overhead.

Experiment 7: Comparison with BAID.

Experiment 8: MCP Governance Proxy Demo.

To validate real-world applicability, we implement a complete MCP governance proxy in Python (520 lines) that interposes between an MCP client (agent) and MCP server (tool provider). The proxy enforces all three governance requirements: G1 via skills manifest hash verification against the agent’s certificate, G2 via reproducibility commitment tracking, and G3 via a hash-chain interaction ledger with Ed25519-signed records. We test 5 live attack scenarios:

All attacks are detected in real-time. Over 1,000 governed calls, the proxy achieves mean governance overhead of 120 µs/call (median: 106 µs, p99: 432 µs), throughput of 8,195 governed calls/sec, and all ledger records pass integrity verification. This confirms that the framework provides real-time protection with overhead well below the latency of typical MCP calls (50–500 ms).

7.3 Attack Scenario Evaluation

We implement 12 attack scenarios as automated tests: 9 structural governance attacks as Rust unit tests (774 lines), 5 end-to-end scenarios via the MCP governance proxy demo (520 lines), and 3 runtime behavioral attacks informed by the Nemotron-AIQ dataset [45] (which demonstrates 100% attack success rates without structural defenses). Table 7 summarizes results.

7.4 End-to-End Multi-Agent Pipeline

Experiments 1–8 evaluate individual governance operations in isolation. To validate the framework under realistic conditions, we deploy the full A2Auth governance stack across a multi-agent pipeline where agents coordinate, delegate tasks, invoke tools via MCP, and pass results through the interaction ledger. This experiment measures: (a) end-to-end governance overhead as a fraction of pipeline latency, (b) scaling behavior from 5 to 20 agents, (c) attack detection in situ, and (d) comparison with three baselines. The implementation uses the Rust agent-trust-kit SDK exposed to Python via PyO3 FFI, with agents making real Anthropic Claude API calls.

Pipeline architecture (Figure 5). We implement an AI Research Assistant pipeline: a user submits a research query; a Coordinator agent (T1_HIGH) orchestrates five specialist agents—Research (T2), Analysis (T2), Writer (T2), Review (T3_MONITORED), and Fact-Checker (T2)—each with a distinct skills manifest and reproducibility commitment. The trust tree has depth 3 (Root CA →\to Human →\to Coordinator →\to Workers), with the Coordinator’s max_delegation_depth=2{}=2 and all workers at depth 0 (cannot delegate). A single pipeline run traverses 21 steps: 10 tool calls (7 LLM invocations + 3 non-LLM tools), 11 inter-agent communications (task assignments and result deliveries), each producing a bilaterally-signed ledger record with capability verification and reproducibility commitment.

Experiment 9a: Governance overhead. Table 8 breaks down governance cost per pipeline run. Each operation’s latency is consistent with the micro-benchmarks from Experiments 1–4; the end-to-end cost is their composition.

Governance adds 10.8 ms to a pipeline that takes ∼{\sim}8.7 s with real Claude API calls (7 LLM inferences at ∼{\sim}1.2 s each + 3 non-LLM tools at ∼{\sim}100 ms each). The overhead of 0.12% is dominated by ledger appends (87% of governance cost), confirming that the cryptographic operations themselves (hashing, signing, verification) are negligible relative to I/O-bound agent workloads.

Experiment 9b: Scaling behavior. We scale the pipeline from 5 to 20 agents by instantiating parallel specialist groups: the Large configuration uses 4 Research agents (handling sub-queries in parallel), 4 Analysis agents, 3 Writer agents, 3 Review agents, 3 Fact-Checkers, 2 Coordinators (primary + sub-coordinator), and 1 Aggregator. Table 9 shows that per-agent governance cost remains approximately constant.

Total governance cost scales linearly with ledger entries (R2>0.99R^{2}>0.99), but per-agent cost increases only 27% when quadrupling the agent count (1.81 ms →\to 2.30 ms). This near-constant per-agent cost arises because each agent’s governance operations—certificate verification, capability checking, ledger append—are independent of the total number of agents in the pipeline. The slight increase comes from deeper trust chains in the Large configuration (depth 4 vs. depth 3) adding one extra signature verification per activation. Ledger storage grows at ∼{\sim}250 bytes per entry; even the 20-agent pipeline produces only 23.8 KB per run, confirming that commitment-only storage (§5) is practical for long-running agent workflows.

Experiment 9c: End-to-end attack detection. We inject five attacks into the live 5-agent pipeline, each targeting a different governance layer. Unlike the unit-level tests in Table 7, these attacks occur mid-pipeline with real inter-agent data flow.

All five attacks are detected. E2E-1 (Research Agent’s MCP server advertises an extra file_write tool at runtime) is caught in 5 µs by the skills manifest hash check—the cheapest possible defense. E2E-2 (Analysis Agent secretly uses Haiku 4.5 instead of declared Sonnet 4) requires replay verification; the framework’s comparison cost is 13 µs, but the dominant cost is LLM re-inference (∼{\sim}1.2 s). E2E-3 (Writer Agent attempts to delegate to an unregistered “Formatter” agent) is blocked at two levels: the Writer’s max_depth=0{}=0 prevents delegation, and the Formatter has no valid certificate chain. E2E-4 (attacker modifies the Research→\toAnalysis result record’s output commitment) is detected immediately by hash-chain verification. E2E-5 (poisoned search results propagate through Research→\toAnalysis→\toWriter) demonstrates multi-layer detection: ledger forensics traces the provenance chain through 3 hops to the injected web_search call, replay verification confirms divergence, and if the poisoned tool is a code-level replacement, capability binding catches the hash mismatch before execution.

Across 100 clean pipeline runs (500 total governed tool calls, 2,100 ledger entries), zero false positives are observed.

Experiment 9d: Baseline comparison. We evaluate the same five E2E attacks against three baselines: (1) no governance (raw MCP), (2) MCP with OAuth 2.1 (standard MCP authentication per specification), and (3) MCP with OpenTelemetry traces (observability-only, no cryptographic integrity). Table 11 summarizes results.

OAuth 2.1 provides identity authentication but not capability binding: it verifies who the agent is, not what tools it currently has. OpenTelemetry provides observability but not integrity: OTEL span trees log tool calls and parent-child relationships, but as demonstrated by analysis of 10,796 Nemotron-AIQ traces (§5), OTEL records contain no hash chains, no cryptographic signatures, and no identity binding—any field can be silently modified. A2Auth’s three governance layers (G1+G2+G3) provide the only configuration that detects all five attack types, with governance overhead below 0.2% of pipeline latency.

8 Limitations and Future Work

8.1 Scope of Contribution

Our contribution is a governance framework, not novel cryptographic primitives. The individual building blocks—X.509 certificates, SHA-256, Ed25519, hash chains—are standard. The novelty lies in (a) identifying the capability-context separation as the principled boundary for agent governance, (b) showing that composing standard mechanisms along this boundary enforces G1–G3 with negligible overhead, and (c) demonstrating this is practically achievable. We view this as analogous to Certificate Transparency [16], which composes Merkle trees and gossip protocols—neither novel individually—into infrastructure that fundamentally changed how the web PKI operates. The security proofs are intentionally straightforward reductions to standard assumptions (collision resistance, EUF-CMA); the contribution is in what to build, not in new ways to prove things.

8.2 Capability Binding Limitations

Capability-context boundary. Our sharp boundary has edge cases: a “code execution” tool can effectively acquire new capabilities through composition (e.g., downloading and running arbitrary scripts). Our framework guarantees that the registered capability set has not changed, but the effective attack surface within a fixed capability envelope can still be large. Complementary approaches (sandboxing, taint tracking, output filtering) are needed to govern behavior within the envelope. We view capability binding and intra-capability governance as orthogonal layers: the former ensures the attack surface is known; the latter constrains behavior within it.

Closed-source binding. For closed-source models and tools, the skills hash captures configuration metadata (name, version, API schema), not implementation code. A provider could change implementation without changing the public descriptor. Reproducibility verification provides a complementary detection mechanism: implementation changes that alter behavior will be detected via replay divergence.

Re-signing frequency. Mitigated through wildcard tool categories, short-lived auto-renewable certificates, and the empirical observation that tool configurations change far less frequently than user context.

8.3 Reproducibility Limitations and Graceful Degradation

Reproducibility is a design constraint, not a universal guarantee. Our framework makes explicit what is often implicit: non-reproducible agent behavior is non-verifiable. This is not a limitation unique to our approach—it applies to any verification scheme not based on trusted hardware. For high-assurance deployments, this means agents should be configured for deterministic output (structured formats, temperature==0, fixed seeds). Our empirical results (§7) show that code-generating agents already satisfy this constraint perfectly, and the separation between same-model and cross-model distributions (11.5×11.5\times) provides robust detection even for prose tasks.

Graceful degradation under partial G2. Our multi-provider experiment (§7, Experiment 5c) reveals that model determinism varies by over an order of magnitude: from CharMatch==0.987 (Haiku 4.5) to 0.169 (Kimi K2.5). This raises a practical question: what security guarantees hold when some agents use low-determinism models?

When G2 is unavailable (reproducibility commitment =𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑒=\mathit{none}), the framework degrades to G1+G3 only. Table 12 characterizes the precise security impact.

G1+G3 alone protect against 9 of 12 attack types. The three attacks that require G2—model substitution (ATK-2), cascading injection via model compromise (ATK-10/11 when the injection occurs through model replacement rather than tool replacement), and output exfiltration via model tampering (ATK-12)—share a common structure: the attacker operates within a valid capability envelope by substituting the computational process itself. Signing proves attribution; only G2 proves computational fidelity.

Chain-level degradation. The Chain Verifiability Theorem (§4.8) establishes a stronger result: a G2==none agent at an interior position breaks behavioral verification for all downstream nodes. This means the true cost of deploying a low-determinism model at a coordinator position is not merely that the coordinator itself is unverifiable, but that the entire sub-tree it governs loses G2 protection. The framework’s three commitment levels (full/statistical/none) are thus not equivalent—their security implications depend critically on chain position.

Statistical vs. computational security. Token-level reproducibility provides statistical rather than computational security. However, the Bounded Divergence Theorem (§4.7) shows this gap is operationally small: sufficient replay verification transforms statistical detection into a provable safety certificate. An adversary who fine-tunes a model to pass nn diverse replay checks has produced a model that is (n,ϵ)(n,\epsilon)-indistinguishable from the original, with ϵ\epsilon decreasing exponentially in nn. Future work will explore semantic similarity (embedding cosine distance) as a verification metric, which may provide tighter separation bounds and is robust to paraphrase-level variation.

Provider cooperation. Replay verification requires access to the same model version. Organizations should negotiate replay rights as part of service agreements. Deterministic inference providers [6] eliminate this dependency entirely.

8.4 Trust Infrastructure Limitations

Non-agent node compromise. We assume non-agent nodes (CAs, humans, organizations) are uncompromised. Standard PKI mitigations apply: Certificate Transparency logs, hardware trust anchors (TPM 2.0), and multi-party issuance protocols. Ledger operator trust. The current single-operator ledger relies on bilateral signing for tamper evidence. A multi-operator design with consensus is possible but introduces latency overhead. Application-layer data flow. Our framework governs agent identity and capability, not the content of data flows. Complementary approaches (data-flow taint tracking, differential privacy) address this orthogonal concern.

8.5 Future Work

Hardware-attested agent identity (TPM 2.0, TEEs) for stronger G2 guarantees without provider cooperation. Embedding-based semantic similarity for reproducibility verification with formal threshold analysis. Cross-protocol capability governance beyond MCP/A2A. AI-assisted certificate issuance to reduce operational burden. Dynamic trust calibration from ledger history, enabling trust scores to evolve based on observed agent behavior.

9 Related Work

We organize related work along the four-layer landscape.

Identity Platforms. Keyfactor [19] and HID Global [20] propose X.509 for agents but without tool binding. SPIFFE/SPIRE [21, 22] provides workload identity. CyberArk [37] extends PAM to agents.

Authorization Frameworks. OIDC-A [4] extends OpenID Connect with agent claims. South et al. [3] propose Agent-ID Tokens (ICML 2025). Agentic JWT [10] defines delegation with temporal constraints.

Runtime Gateways. Gravitee [40] and Lasso [41] provide MCP proxies with per-call enforcement—fundamentally stateless.

Governance Platforms. Credo AI [42] maintains agent registries at the documentation layer.

Verifiable Execution. BAID [2] provides zkVM-based verification (∼{\sim}120 s per proof). DiFR [1] demonstrates inference near-determinism. EigenAI [6] achieves 100% deterministic inference. Attestable Audits [7] uses TEEs.

Classical Trust Management. PolicyMaker [12], KeyNote [13], SPKI/SDSI [14], F-PKI [16], ARPKI [17].

Agent Protocols. A2A [8] provides agent communication. MCP enables agent-tool interaction with OAuth 2.1.

Agent Governance Frameworks. Cheng et al. [43] propose a three-pillar model (transparency, accountability, trustworthiness) as a conceptual governance framework. Allegrini et al. [44] formalize 31 task-lifecycle properties in CTL/LTL but address operational correctness rather than cryptographic governance. Ghosh et al. [45] propose an operational safety framework with agent red-teaming probes (ARP), policy-based tool scoping, and OpenTelemetry-based audit trails, validated through a 10,796-trace dataset (Nemotron-AIQ) covering 22 security attack templates and 13 content-safety categories against NVIDIA’s AI-Q research assistant. Their empirical results demonstrate that without guardrails, all 2,596 security attacks succeed (100%), and 20% of 2,800 safety attacks propagate to the final output—providing compelling evidence for the inadequacy of relying solely on model alignment. However, their OTEL-based audit trails lack cryptographic integrity: span linkage is purely referential (no hash chaining), spans carry no agent identity binding (no certificates), and full plaintext I/O is stored (no privacy preservation). Our framework addresses these gaps with a formally verified, hash-chain-linked, bilaterally signed interaction ledger (Section 5). Furthermore, their “signed schemas” and “per-call capability tokens” remain design principles without cryptographic specification or formal proofs. Raza et al. [28] adapt TRiSM for agentic multi-agent systems.

Regulatory Landscape. The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) requires traceability but lacks agent-specific implementing acts [33]. NIST CAISI [26] is developing agent standards. CSA [24, 25] proposes agentic trust frameworks.

10 Conclusion

AI agents increasingly acquire capabilities at runtime, yet no existing framework enforces the three governance requirements—capability integrity, behavioral verifiability, and interaction auditability—that a trustworthy agent ecosystem demands.

We addressed this through the capability-context separation principle and three mechanisms: capability-bound certificates (G1), reproducibility commitments (G2), and a verifiable interaction ledger (G3). We formalized nine security properties (including chain verifiability: behavioral verification is a chain property broken by any unverifiable interior agent), implemented the framework in Rust with 97 µs verification and <<1 ns capability binding overhead (∼1,200,000×{\sim}1{,}200{,}000\times faster than BAID), validated reproducibility across 9 models from 7 providers (F1=0.876F_{1}=0.876 multi-provider, F1=0.990F_{1}=0.990 single-provider), and verified 12 attack scenarios—including runtime behavioral attacks validated against NVIDIA Nemotron-AIQ traces—with specific, traceable detection mechanisms. An end-to-end evaluation deploying the full governance stack across a 5-to-20-agent pipeline with real LLM calls confirms 0.12% overhead, sub-linear per-agent scaling, and detection of all in-situ attacks with zero false positives—while three baselines (no governance, OAuth 2.1, OpenTelemetry) detect none.

Our framework fills the stateful, capability-aware governance gap between identity platforms and runtime gateways. As the EU AI Act’s high-risk provisions take effect and NIST develops agent-specific standards, the need for cryptographic infrastructure enforcing G1–G3 will only grow.

We release the core mechanisms as an open-source SDK (agent-trust-kit) to enable ecosystem adoption.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
